abstract: Especially as regards Commonwealth restrictions, Ireland's immigration policy has been seen as (surreptitiously) dependent on UK policy. Although the Common Travel Area imposed serious limits, Irish discretion was in fact significant and restrictive. In 1948–9 the United Kingdom secured Ireland's public commitment to extend reciprocal citizenship rights to all the Commonwealth, notwithstanding its secession, but Ireland avoided this vis-à-vis the ‘new’ Commonwealth and left its aliens exemption law deliberately opaque. Whilst broadly mirroring the UK Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1962, Ireland retained apartheid South Africa as partially privileged and only comprehensively exempted British citizens born within the United Kingdom. From 1973, the United Kingdom largely abandoned any privileged treatment but, in entirely removing this in 1975 and selectively imposing visas from 1976, Ireland went beyond even this. These divergences reflected that, compared to the United Kingdom, it had left an increasingly diverse Commonwealth in 1949 and had a stronger homogenous nationalism.

title: A Most ‘Valuable Class’: The Shetland Female Emigration Society and the Emigration of Single Women to South Australia and Tasmania in the early 1850s
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Emigration, diaspora & return; Language & multilingualism; Migrant communities, identity & family life

abstract: This article examines the reasons behind the formation of the little-known Shetland Female Emigration Society and its reception in the Australian colonies. Much has been written about emigration from Scotland and, even more extensively, about female emigration from the United Kingdom in the second half of the nineteenth century. The question of female emigration from Scotland at the time has, by contrast, attracted little attention from scholars so far, even though the country represents a particularly interesting case-study, offering as it did candidates for emigration that differed widely from one region to another in linguistic, religious and ethnic terms. Yet, the SFES, which was launched in 1850 to help in the emigration of young and single women to South Australia and Tasmania, presents the particularity of having offered a Presbyterian, Scandinavian, English-speaking set of emigrants whose moral, domestic and religious qualities made them stand out from their Celtic (and Roman Catholic) Highland and Irish counterparts. Drawing on a wide range of primary sources, this paper looks at the conditions in which this philanthropic society was launched, at the intersection of Scottish, British and Australian needs. It also, and mostly, argues that the reception of such schemes must not only be analysed through the lens of gender, famine-relief and imperialist goals, but also through that of a cultural, religious and ethnic bias.

abstract: This chapter details the history of the Irish Immigration Reform Movement (IIRM), whose advocacy on behalf of unauthorized Irish immigrants in the 1980s produced meaningful legislative reforms that countered immigration restriction. The IIRM succeeded by building empathy for the plight of unauthorized Irish immigrants through media coverage and by working with sympathetic policymakers. They made arguments about Irish immigrants’ historical contributions to the United States, but they also embraced a more expansive argument about the centrality of independent immigration and diversity to the American story. As a result, they were able to change public perceptions and state policies on immigration, something that was unusual in a context of rising nativism and renewed focus on cracking down on unauthorized immigration. Yet the scripts they deployed to build empathy and create access to visas reproduced ideas about belonging along lines of race.

title: Urbanization and genetic homogenization in the medieval Low Countries revealed through a ten-century paleogenomic study of the city of Sint-Truiden
authors: Owyn Beneker; Ludovica Molinaro; Meriam Guellil; Stefania Sasso; Helja Kabral; Biancamaria Bonucci; Noah Gaens; Eugenia D'Atanasio; Massimo Mezzavilla; Hélios Delbrassine; Linde Braet; Bart Lambert et al.

abstract: Processes shaping the formation of the present-day population structure in highly urbanized Northern Europe are still poorly understood. Gaps remain in our understanding of when and how currently observable regional differences emerged and what impact city growth, migration, and disease pandemics during and after the Middle Ages had on these processes. We perform low-coverage sequencing of the genomes of 338 individuals spanning the eighth to the eighteenth centuries in the city of Sint-Truiden in Flanders, in the northern part of Belgium. The early/high medieval Sint-Truiden population was more heterogeneous, having received migrants from Scotland or Ireland, and displayed less genetic relatedness than observed today between individuals in present-day Flanders. We find differences in gene variants associated with high vitamin D blood levels between individuals with Gaulish or Germanic ancestry. Although we find evidence of a Yersinia pestis infection in 5 of the 58 late medieval burials, we were unable to detect a major population-scale impact of the second plague pandemic on genetic diversity or on the elevated differentiation of immunity genes. This study reveals that the genetic homogenization process in a medieval city population in the Low Countries was protracted for centuries. Over time, the Sint-Truiden population became more similar to the current population of the surrounding Limburg province, likely as a result of reduced long-distance migration after the high medieval period, and the continuous process of local admixture of Germanic and Gaulish ancestries which formed the genetic cline observable today in the Low Countries.

title: Stages in the development of terminology studies in national and foreign linguistics
themes: Ukrainian temporary protection; Emigration, diaspora & return; Language & multilingualism; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life

abstract: The aim of this article is to systematize the existing research on the history of the development of Ukrainian and global terminology studies and terminology. It analyzes both contemporary and earlier research on the history of terminology studies and terminology. The article examines and characterizes each stage of the development of terminology studies in Ukraine: the initial or “pre-scientific” stage; the period of formation of modern terminology and scientific language; the period of its rapid development in the 1920s and the early 1930s; the period of decline marked by convergence of the Ukrainian language with Russian; the modern period. The contribution of the Ukrainian diaspora to terminology studies is also highlighted, particularly during the time when scholars in Ukraine faced restrictions in their work. Additionally, the article explores the corresponding history and periodization of the development of global terminology studies. The key stages of global terminology development are identified as follows: the initial period – from ancient times to the 17th–18th centuries; the period of terminology enrichment, with early attempts of systematization and regulation; the early modern and contemporary periods of terminology studies. The article provides a detailed analysis of the development of terminology studies in the 20th century — a formative period of terminology studies as scientific discipline. This stage is examined within both the Ukrainian and global contexts. Special emphasis is focused on the contemporary stage of terminology studies in Ukraine and globally. Particular attention is given to modern trends in terminology studies, including communicative, semiotic, and cognitive approaches, historiography, and current issues of terminology standardization and unification. The article provides detailed research of current issues in the standardization and normalization of terminology and terminography. The concepts of terminology and terminological system are investigated within the framework of contemporary linguistics. The development of specific national terminology systems is also examined, including those of Czech, Slovak, Austrian, French, Irish, Icelandic, Latvian, Lithuanian, Malay, and Israeli.

title: This Racial War: Constructing Transnational Whiteness in the Newspaper Poems of the South African War, 1899–1902
themes: Naturalisation & citizenship; Health, care & health workforce; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Language & multilingualism; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: only ambiguous migration terms; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: A survey of poems published in British and colonial English-language newspapers during the South African War (1899–1902) reveals an almost complete silence about the Black Africans affected by the war. This essay considers what newspaper poets meant by designating the conflict ‘this racial war’, exploring their contributions to a notion of transnational whiteness. There are doubts and inconsistencies in newspaper poets’ presentation of kinship relationships across the settler empire, particularly with respect to Ireland. Questions about Indian colonial citizenship likewise call attention to the policing of Greater Britain’s racialized boundaries. The prospect of peace and the need to incorporate South Africa as a white Dominion required Boer whiteness to be reframed. Whiteness emerges as a concept under construction, unstable and incoherent, both cause and effect of imperial war. Nonetheless, newspaper poets’ appeals to race and whiteness as neutral concepts are fundamental to the structures of imperial racism.

abstract: Abstract “A guy needs somebody to be near him. A guy goes nuts if he ain’t got nobody. Don’t make no difference who the guy is, long’s he’s with you. Europe is seeing unprecedented growth in the ageing population along with an influx of migrants. This paper explores this issue from the perspective of the ethical component of society to address this issue. There is an epidemic of loneliness sweeping across Europe. The aim of this scoping review is an attempt to discuss how loneliness can impact on physical, cognitive and emotional health across the lifespan. It is not an exhaustive review. The objective is an attempt to reflect how as a society the epidemic of loneliness has crept in without adequate policies and procedures put in place by Governments to combat this 21st century phenomenon. Methodology utilized a scoping review of the literature in relation to loneliness. It explores the connection of loneliness with a decrease in physical and mental health for citizens. title: Contesting American citizenship on stage: sexuality, ethnicity, and the reception of The Playboy of the Western World
themes: Naturalisation & citizenship; Asylum, international protection & reception; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; only ambiguous migration terms; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: ABSTRACT J. M. Synge’s The Playboy of the Western World provoked polarised reactions during its 1911 U.S. tour. Set against the historical backdrop of the Progressive Era, a time when sexual self-discipline was deemed essential to new American citizenship, the play directly confronted this norm. This article employs a performative perspective of citizenship to argue that the play served as a nexus of intersectionality, where gender, ethnicity, and class interacted to shape civic identities. For Irish American communities, women’s sexual decency was pivotal to their transition to full citizenship. To that end, organised Irish protesters staged riots to assert their “civisme.” Conversely, white, middle-class club women embraced the play, strategically adopting its controversial portrayals of women’s sexuality as a means of advocating for their own citizenship rights. These riots revealed the tension between ethnic citizenship and women’s suffrage, and ultimately illuminated how these competing priorities shaped audience responses.

title: The making and meaning of Celtic FC and Notre Dame Football, 1887–1931: critically comparing two sporting institutions in their national and diasporic context
themes: Emigration, diaspora & return; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: ABSTRACT For nearly a century, concise parallels have been drawn between the cultural meanings and experiences of Celtic Football Club and Notre Dame Football (‘The Fighting Irish’). Despite such analogies, no scholarship or popular literature exists which compares the early historical development of these two footballing institutions, both in their national and diasporic context. Nevertheless, as will now be demonstrated, when such an approach is undertaken, a subtle but salient difference appears to be detectable. Celtic FC quickly became the main sporting and secular symbol of the Irish Catholic diaspora in Scotland, whereas Notre Dame Football came to represent and symbolise Catholic America, with its prominent Irish dimension. On the one hand, such a nuanced difference speaks to the contrasting sporting landscapes that both teams operated within, as well as their varying institutional backdrops. However, on the other, the distinction also says something about the intersecting diasporic trajectory of Irish Catholics and other Roman Catholics in Scotland and the United States, at least before 1931. Crucially, such conclusions further validate the importance of viewing diaspora as a living and dialectical experience, rooted in the relationships between places, people, and agency over time.

abstract: Abstract This chapter focuses on Irish-language publishing in the Irish-American diaspora from the late nineteenth century to the early twenty-first. The author argues that most twentieth-century Irish-language publications in the USA came in the form of books for academic purposes (including editions of classic Irish texts) and bilingual periodicals containing both original and reprinted materials. The published books mainly include reprints of Irish-language primers, dictionaries, and anthologies previously published in Dublin and London, and some translations—mainly targeted at American adults learning Irish. The periodicals reviewed here range from An Gaodhal/The Gael in the late nineteenth century to its modern reincarnation as An Gael (2009–). The author includes in his account Irish-language columns, at least one of which (Barra Ó Donnabháin’s contributions to the Irish Echo, New York) has been collected and edited into a full-length book.

abstract: Among the possessions that Irish-born Anne Trotter packed in her trunk to start a new life in Australia was her needlework specimen book. Anne, who arrived in the Port Phillip District in 1844, was one of many assisted migrants that were given a passage to Australia as part of the government’s immigration schemes. Anne’s needlework book, which was donated to Museums Victoria in 2014 by a descendant and includes various plain sewing exercises and finely-stitched miniature shirts, provides an insight into the formal schooling provided to young working-class women in nineteenth century Ireland and the skills that they brought to Australia. This article discusses the context of the needlework book and posits its value to a young female emigrant.

title: Mobilising Xenophobia and Making Colonialism at the British Cape of Good Hope: Emigrants, Africans, and Repealers in the Politics of the 1849 Anti-Convict Movement
themes: Emigration, diaspora & return
venue: Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines the politics of the 1849 anti-convict movement that emerged in the British Cape Colony in southern Africa in response to the designation of the colony as a penal settlement and the impending arrival of three hundred British convicts on board the ship Neptune. It argues that anti-convict political agitation was a form of popular xenophobia, in which foreignness was assigned to ‘convicts’ rather than to a specific national, ethnic, or racial origin. Within this popular xenophobia, Cape colonists invoked frames of reference that encompassed their local, racialised politics of colonial expansion as well as knowledge of a wider imperial world, particularly Ireland. In the Cape’s xenophobic mobilisation, we see how local and global frames of reference were melded and politicised as the settler public sought to constitute itself against perceived threats of ‘outsiders’, including convicted felons and Africans. The ‘convict crisis’ exposes multiple scales of historical and political context, which simultaneously localise the meaning of colonialism and globalise the patterns of knowledge that informed colonial politics. This history underscores local and political variations of colonial relationships, rather than systemic and institutional modes of colonialism, through interrogating how Cape colonists envisioned, rationalised, and acted on their ‘colonial project.’

title: “She’s not the full shilling”: insanity and redemption in William Trevor’s Reading Turgenev
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Health, care & health workforce

abstract: ABSTRACT Throughout his œuvre, William Trevor frequently explores the disorders of the human mind, with his Irish writings often depicting deviance, mental illness, and madness as responses to suffering and loss. In Reading Turgenev (1991), this focus is embodied in Mary Louise Dallon’s presumed madness, which shapes both the novella’s themes and its narrative structure. Partly set in 1950s Ireland – a period marked by peak asylum confinement – the novella critiques institutionalisation through narrative delirium and multifocal storytelling, unfolding like a mosaic rather than following a linear chronology. Through an examination of how insanity disrupts the linear concept of time, the intertextual connections to Turgenev’s writings, and the influence of Mary Louise’s experiences on her perceptions and thoughts, this article suggests that Trevor’s novella slides between the phenomenological and the realist, presenting a heroine who oscillates between madness and redemption.

title: Turbulent Waters, or the Sublime Object of Subalternity

abstract: Abstract:Mark Twain's "Day at Niagara" (1869) concludes with a notorious moment of misrecognition, in which Twain's buffoonish narrator mistakes a group of Irish immigrants for Indigenous people. This essay argues that this misrecognition and its contradictory reception history exemplify representational dilemmas that continue to haunt contemporary scholarship. The three monographs under review, all of which are authored by white scholars engaged with ethnic and Indigenous studies, are indicative of these ongoing quandaries. Rifkin, Stanciu, and Zaborskis strive to navigate a treacherous course between liberal modes of representation and a romanticized refusal to represent subaltern agency as they engage with wide-ranging archives of texts produced by racialized and/or Indigenous people. In their successes and failures in this endeavor, they dramatize some of American studies' most profound unresolved tensions.

title: Navigating Ireland’s ‘ambivalent heritage’ of nationalism and empire: a Corkonian’s journey, 1849–1901

abstract: Abstract It was by chance that John Morrogh (1849–1901) became an imperial player. Leaving Ireland as an almost penniless young man moulded by the Catholic nationalism of the Christian Brothers, he joined the early diamond rush to Kimberley, South Africa, and returned home twenty years later a director of Cecil Rhodes’s De Beers Consolidated Diamond Mines. He joined the Irish Parliamentary Party (IPP) and his diamond fortune eased his path to a seat in the House of Commons. As the IPP fragmented, he took the side of the anti-Parnellite, Tim Healy, until he resigned his seat and returned to Cork where he became an influential figure in business and local government. This article traces the fortunes and sensibilities of an Irish migrant who in many ways exemplifies Ireland’s ‘ambivalent heritage’ of nationalism and empire. 1

title: In Darkest Queensland: A Comparative Zooarchaeological Analysis of Chinese and British Migrants in Frog’s Hollow, a Nineteenth-Century Brisbane Neighborhood
themes: Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: By the late nineteenth century, Queensland was the most ethnically diverse Australian colony and the most severely racially exclusionary. Despite this, to date no zooarchaeological studies have investigated how food choice reflected and reinforced these social dynamics in Queensland or elsewhere across post-European settlement Australia. This study presents a comparative and contextual zooarchaeological analysis of two late nineteenth-century deposits in Brisbane’s "Frog’s Hollow," an ethnically diverse and working class area in the colony’s capital city. This study illustrates the social embeddedness of food choices, and highlights how local influences shaped emerging group identities relating to these choices. The Chinese residents were actively choosing familiar and culturally important foods such as pork, poultry and fish, even enthusiastically consuming expensive pork over the cheaper mutton and beef, while taking advantage of marine resources likely supplied via a Chinese-run fishing village on the outskirts of town. Similarly, the British residents were enthusiastically supporting a local European-run oyster industry, while focusing predominantly on meat-dense cuts of mutton. Mutton was a familiar and affordable source of meat with increasing cultural significance to the predominantly British and Irish population of the colony, and Australia, as a longstanding source of economic success via the colonial wool industries. Here I argue that familiar foods were important for both cultural groups to (re)construct and maintain a sense of cultural and social identity. However, the evidence also shows experimentation, the aspirational associations of a meat-centric diet, and how social networks, communities, and local availability can influence food choice.

title: Insanity and the Insane in Post-Famine Ireland
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Health, care & health workforce; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life; Population, flows & statistics
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Between 1317 and 1870 the British government in Ireland, through the chief secretary’s office in Dublin, directed the establishment of twenty-two district lunatic asylums in Ireland. Founded at a time when the government wa3 attempting to bring order to Ireland through the estab­ lishment of a police force and a system of poor relief, primarily institutional, the asylums were initially welcomed by local gentry, clergy and judicial authorities. But the unceasing growth of asylum admissions after the Famine, together with the failure of the asylum to restore more than a small proportion of inmates to society, provoked increasing local discontent with the institutions. Central government sought to maintain local responsibility for standards while ratepayers’ representatives pressed for the government to take over the financial responsibility for the insane. In this situation, the democratisation of Irish local government in 1898 further ’politicised’ the management of asylums, with questions of finance and local control dominating their administration to the war. Institutionalisation of a growing proportion of the Irish population proceeded particularly through judicial committal. Magistrates, police and doctors used the provisions of the law to confine men and women who were brought to them by their relatives and friends. A law which had been intended only for the detention of the ’dangerous lunatic’ became the routine mode of dealing with a variety of ills from alcoholism to family violence. Within the asylums, the uncertainty as to the basis of an individual inmate’s condition was reflected in the variety of largely unsuccessful therapies, ’moral’ and physical. Even the possibility of organising an ordered environment, subject to the direction of the medical superintendent, the object of the asylum’s structure, failed in the face of over-crowding and institutional inertia. Over the lives of the insane presided doctors who gradually established themselves professionally as psychia­ trists. By the end of the century, in spite of their formal dominance in treatment and control, the psychiatrists had failed to establish a practice which could cope with the increasing institutional pressures on them. Their pessimism concerning the seemingly intractable problem of insanity was matched in Ireland and Britain by an alarm among lay observers at the growth in numbers of the insane. An examin­ ation of the statistical evidence for Ireland suggests that institutiona.lisa.tion proceeded apace with rural decline characterised by high emigration, falling marriage rates and an ageing population. The ’increase of lunacy’ had become a symbol as well as a reflection of the social condition of Ireland after the Famine.

title: Yankee Doodle Paddy and Uncle Sammy: Ethnic Patriotism in Boston's Irish Catholic and Jewish Communities During World War I
themes: Naturalisation & citizenship; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Language & multilingualism; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This article examines how Boston's Irish Catholic and Jewish communities—the city's largest and most influential non-Protestant groups—navigated the pressures of ethnic identity and “100 percent Americanism” during World War I. Using a comparative local lens, it argues that the war fostered “ethnic patriotism” as a shared strategy through which immigrants claimed civic belonging while balancing distinct ethno-religious loyalties. Through enlistment, Liberty Loan drives, and wartime relief work, each group asserted their Americanness while translating Catholic social teaching and Jewish ethics into a civic language aligned with Wilsonian democracy and self-determination. At the same time, they linked transnational causes—Irish independence and Zionism—to American ideals, portraying nationalism abroad as consistent with loyalty at home. Yet ethnic patriotism was contested: class, generation, and ideology divided moderates from militants, while labor radicals challenged middle-class respectability politics. The unrest of 1917 to 1919 exposed the limits of inclusion amid persistent Yankee prejudice and the conditional nature of acceptance. Together, these communities’ wartime experiences reveal Americanization as a process of mutual transformation rather than one-sided assimilation. World War I thus emerges as a crucible in which pluralism was forged—contentiously and locally—redefining Americanness as a civic bond between heritage and citizenship.

title: THE CONTRIBUTION OF THE IRISH DIASPORA MEMBERS TO THE FORMATION OF AMERICAN POLITICAL PHILOSOPHY
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migrant communities, identity & family life

abstract:
The article revealsthe comprehensive influence of ethnic Irish and
Irish Americans on the development of the key aspects of the political culture
and philosophy of the United States. It emphasizes the insufficient study of this
topic in Russian academia and the importance of a comprehensive approach to
evaluating the contribution of individual ethnic communities to the formation
of a unique model of American political philosophy, based on a combination of
ideas of freedom, equality, and civic participation. The author analyzesin detail
the waves of Irish migration, beginning with the Great Famine in 1845–1852,
examines the complex socio-economic conditions that led to the active involvement of the Irish diaspora in the political life of the country, and explains why
politics became the main social elevator for their self-realization. Starting with
the examples of the activities of prominent Irish figures – from the emergence
of the “Jacksonian tradition”, to which John O’Sullivan contributed and until
the formation of the phenomena of political machines and bossism – the article
traces the unique Irish contribution to shaping the principles of American
democracy, equal opportunity, pragmatism, and political mobilization of the
lower classes of society. Special attention is paid to the divisions within the
Irish diaspora itself (the Catholics and Protestants, as well as the Scots-Irish
elements), their different approaches to political strategies and integration.
The article also analyzes the Irish-initiated labor movements and participation
in the Civil War, where the integration of the military, trade union, and political practices allowed this group to consolidate social capital and influence the
long-term processes of American identity and nationalism.

title: Chicago's Irish Nationalists: From Civil Rights to Bloody Sunday, 1968–1972
themes: Labour market, work & permits; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: From the mid-1800s onward, Chicago's Irish immigrants played an important role in supporting both physical force and constitutional nationalist organizations in their ancestral homeland. This tradition of assistance declined significantly after the partition of Ireland in 1921. Most of Chicago's Irish community saw the Irish Free State's dominion status as a significant step toward eventual freedom. In addition, the 1924 Immigration Act and onset of the Great Depression cut the city's nationalist groups off from the steady stream of new arrivals from Ireland that had been a source of regeneration for nearly a century. Chicago's post–1945 suburbanization further compounded these trends, breaking the sense of ethnic solidarity that had traditionally driven concern for events in Ireland. This article argues, however, that in the late 1960s, despite all the challenges, Chicago's remaining Irish nationalists were rejuvenated by the outbreak of violence in Northern Ireland. Enraged by what they saw as British oppression, particularly the use of internment without trial and the murder of civil rights demonstrators on Bloody Sunday, they channeled their activism through the Irish Northern Aid Committee (Noraid). In its first two years, Chicago Noraid sent significant amounts of cash to the republican movement in Ireland, helped generate publicity for their cause, and attracted support from a handful of the city's political leaders. Others set up weapons pipelines that provided the Provisional IRA with the military hardware it needed to wage an “armed struggle” that helped bring down the Unionist government in Belfast.

title: Stefan Terlezki and the processes of European integration during 1970–1980s
themes: Ukrainian temporary protection; Health, care & health workforce; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract:
Purpose. The purpose of this article is to examine the place and role of Stefan Terlezki in the processes of European integration during the 1970s and 1980s. Methodology. In writing this scientific article, the authors used the approaches of transnational history, international history, and civilization. The issue is examined in three contexts: the Ukrainian diaspora in Great Britain, the role of Great Britain in the processes of European integration, and London’s policy towards the European Economic Community.

Terlezki was a member of the political group ‘Keep Britain in Europe’ during the referendum held in June 1975. He later served as a member of the House of Commons of the British Parliament (1983–1987) and was a member of the delegation of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland to the Western European Union in 1985–1987.

Scientific novelty. The article introduces archival documents relating to the public, political and diplomatic activities of Stefan Terlezki (1927–2006) into scientific circulation. These materials allow us to analyse the history of European integration, taking into account the Ukrainian question in British and international politics during the Cold War. 

The processes of European integration in the 1970s and 1980s are shown as a period when the Ukrainian people’s struggle for decolonisation against the USSR continued. The example of Stefan Terlezki showed that raising the Ukrainian question in the European dimension was an important but insufficient step, as European politicians knew and understood little about the colonial nature of Moscow’s policy towards the Ukrainian SSR.

Conclusions. The process of conceptual rethinking of the history of European integration is currently underway. A direct participant in these processes in the 1970s and 1980s in the context of Great Britain and Europe was Stefan Terlezki, a representative of the Ukrainian diaspora in the United Kingdom. In the current geopolitical conditions, it is necessary to take into account the experience of advocacy and communication development in the past in order to act now.

title: Eugenio Pacelli and the Vatican’s Irish Plan to Save Baptized Jews (1938–1939)
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Migration policy, law & governance
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Shortly after the enactment in September 1938 of the first of Fascist Italy’s anti-Jewish ‘racial laws’, which mandated the expulsion from the country of all foreign Jews, desperate pleas for help began flooding into the Vatican. The pleas came overwhelmingly from Jews who had been baptised. Vatican secretary of state, Eugenio Pacelli, initially saw in Ireland the best possibility for a solution. Over the next months a thick correspondence developed between Pacelli and the nuncio in Dublin, Paschal Robinson. The nuncio in turn relied on Sir Joseph Glynn, president of Ireland’s St Vincent de Paul Society, to spearhead the resettlement effort. Not long after Pacelli became pope himself in March 1939, Vatican hopes for the Irish plan faded. Vatican ambitions for Ireland foundered on the lack of support among both the Church hierarchy and the general population for helping refugees regarded as Jews, notwithstanding their baptismal status.

title: 'I felt like I just belonged': urban multiculture and black Irish migrants in post-war Britain.
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migrant communities, identity & family life
institutions: School of History, Anthropology, Philosophy and Politics, Queen's University Belfast, 25 University Square, United Kingdom.
screening_note: MANUAL: post-war Irish migrants in Britain
abstract: This article reevaluates historians' understanding of the Irish in post-war Britain from the perspective of a previously unresearched population, black and mixed-race Irish migrants. Writing on the Irish in Britain has lingered on themes such as stereotyping, discrimination, and ethnic profiling. More widely, some historians have framed Irish emigration and the diaspora around motifs of exile and reluctant departure, while others have highlighted the liberating potential of departure. Oral histories with black Irish migrants fall firmly into the latter, emancipatory camp, depicting urban, multicultural Britain as a site of acceptance and belonging. Far from presenting emigration as a reluctant withdrawal from a cherished homeland, Irish people of colour narrated their departure as a liberating exit from an upbringing of alienation and abuse. These findings have wider implications for understanding the dynamics of British multiculture. Black Irish narrators revelled in the anonymity granted by post-war British diversity, which allowed them to discover and embrace their blackness. Some found belonging within the black communities of urban Britain, especially London. Conversely, they faced rejection from Irish diasporic spaces, which were characterized by conservative, Catholic and exclusively white conceptions of Irishness. The article therefore uses previously unexplored narratives to reframe our understanding of the Irish community in Britain and the broader context of urban multiculture in which it existed.

title: Voices across the airwaves: Gendered memories of sports radio in the Irish diaspora
authors: Daithí McMahon; Verónica Posada Álvarez; Julia Giese
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life; Population, flows & statistics
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This article examines the cultural and affective significance of sports radio within the Irish diaspora from the 1960s to the present, tracing its transformation from a communal listening ritual to individualised, digitally mediated practices. Beginning with the historic 1947 All-Ireland Senior Football Championship final, which was broadcast live from New York to Ireland, the study considers how mediated listening has enabled diasporic communities to sustain ties to home and negotiate belonging across borders. Drawing on interviews with a Gaelic football commentator and five diasporic participants in Britain, the USA, and Australia, the article situates radio listening at the intersection of memory, gender, and diaspora studies. While foregrounding radio’s capacity to foster affective co-presence—particularly among men—it interrogates the gendered exclusions embedded in these media rituals. Advancing the concept of ‘multi-axial togetherness’, the article calls for a nuanced understanding of diasporic media flows that accounts for intersecting dimensions of gender, class, and generation.

title: Committal, discharge and varied institutional experiences in the Richmond District Lunatic Asylum, Dublin in the early 20th century: Legislative provisions, clinical cases and the position of ‘mental hospitals’ in Ireland's cultures of confinement
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Health, care & health workforce; Migration policy, law & governance
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Founded in 1810, the Richmond District Lunatic Asylum at Grangegorman, Dublin, Ireland, admitted tens of thousands of patients over the course of almost two centuries. Staff introduced many new treatments for mental illness, ranging from ‘moral management’ in the early 19th century to the biological treatments of the 20th century (e.g. malaria therapy, insulin coma, lobotomy). The Richmond was a model for the network of district asylums established across Ireland during the 19th and early 20th centuries. This article summarises the legislative underpinning of Ireland's high committal rates in the late 19th and early 20th centuries; draws on the Richmond's archive to present two clinical cases of women who were committed to the Richmond in 1907 and 1908 but had different outcomes; and explores the nature of ‘institutional careers’ in Ireland's ‘mental hospital’ system in the early 20th century as one element within Ireland's cultures of confinement during this period.

title: Imperial Politics, the Dominions, and the Irish Question, 1907–21
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Emigration, diaspora & return
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Abstract It has long been recognized that the “Irish Question” was also an imperial question. The vast Irish diaspora in the settler colonies ensured that Home Rule had enormous consequences for the wider empire. But scholars have yet fully to appreciate the part that political elites in the self-governing Dominions played in this story. This article explores the role of colonial statesmen in Anglo-Irish affairs. Figures like Australia’s Billy Hughes or South Africa’s Jan Smuts were able to navigate the emotional complexities of Irish nationalist politics in a manner that transcended British party politics. In the process, they framed “colonial” Home Rule as a compromise between British rule and independence. This article shows how Irish nationalist politics became enmeshed with imperial politics in a manner that blurred the line between the local, national, imperial, and global.

title: Québec, Dublin et la fondation d'universités catholiques dans l'Empire britannique au XIXe siècle
themes: Education, children & young people; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migrant communities, identity & family life
venue: Historical Studies in Education / Revue d'histoire de l'éducation
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Cet article analyse la fondation, au milieu du XIXe siècle, d’universités catholiques dans les villes de Québec et de Dublin, sous l’autorité de l’Église catholique et dans le contexte de l’Empire britannique. L’Université Laval fut fondée dans la ville de Québec et la Catholic University of Ireland, à Dublin, comme des réponses catholiques à la montée de l’éducation supérieure protestante et aux révolutions de 1848. Ces deux universités ouvrirent leurs portes à quelques semaines d’écart, en 1854. Une partie du clergé catholique du Canada et de l’Irlande considéra la création d’universités catholiques comme un moyen de préserver sa religion, minoritaire en Amérique du Nord britannique comme au Royaume-Uni. L’article examine d’abord les projets d’universités catholiques qui prirent forme au Canada et en Irlande dans la première moitié du XIXe siècle. Il met ensuite en évidence le soutien qu’apporta la diaspora irlandaise catholique à la création d’une université catholique à Dublin, en soulignant comment ce soutien favorisa indirectement la fondation de l’Université Laval. L’article se conclut par l’analyse du voyage en Europe effectué en 1852 par Louis-Jacques Casault, supérieur du Séminaire de Québec, afin d’obtenir des chartes auprès de la Couronne britannique et du Saint-Siège pour l’Université Laval. Par ce voyage, des représentants des projets d’universités catholiques de Québec et de Dublin se croisèrent à Rome, où le Saint-Siège se prononça sur ces deux projets en les comparant l’un à l’autre et en évaluant à quel point chacun d’eux risquait de contrarier les autorités politiques du Royaume-Uni. Ce voyage de Casault, qui l’aurait fait notamment s’arrêter en Belgique, indique enfin combien l’Université catholique de Louvain servit de référence à l’époque pour la fondation d’universités catholiques, tant à Québec qu’à Dublin

title: St. Raphael's, Queens: From a Rural to an Urban Parish, 1868–1930
themes: Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Abstract:A one-hundred-foot red brick church steeple looming over the Long Island Expressway signifies New York City's outer boroughs' Catholic history to thousands making their way from Manhattan to JFK airport. The history of St. Raphael Church casts light on an important but neglected aspect of urbanization, namely the experience of Catholics on the urban periphery in the latter nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, years of slow then rapid change amid the intensive fin de siècle expansion of American metropolises. On the mid to late nineteenth-century rural but industrializing periphery of Manhattan, St. Raphael took identity as a predominantly Irish hinterland parish adjoining the Archdiocese of New York's countryside Catholic cemetery. Yet with the propulsive urbanization and industrialization that occurred after the consolidation of Queens County into New York City in 1898, St. Raphael's physical and cultural setting was transformed into an intensely urban identity, constrained by factories and expressways and transformed by the arrival of successive waves of Catholic immigrants.

title: Medieval Manuscripts in Marsh’s Library: An Unintended Collection in Dublin’s First Public Library
authors: L. Cleaver; D. Magnusson; Isabel Tookey
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Abstract:Narcissus Marsh began planning a public library for Dublin at the end of the seventeenth century. By 1704, a library building had been constructed near Saint Patrick’s Cathedral, and Marsh turned his attention to its contents. He planned a collection of 10,000 books “with none but ye most usefull Books in each Faculty and Science.” Marsh was prepared to buy books from London and the Continent and sought advice on what the most appropriate new titles for his library might be. He bought books individually and en bloc, including volumes from the library of the Dublin scholar Dudley Loftus. However, he recognized that buying collections risked adding books that he did not want. Marsh deliberately bought what he called “Oriental” manuscripts, which he left to the Bodleian Library, but a few European volumes remained in Dublin. Among the volumes acquired from Loftus that did not obviously fit Marsh’s plan were a small number of medieval manuscripts. More medieval books were added when, in 1701, Marsh recruited a Huguenot refugee, Elie Bouhéreau, as librarian for the new collection, with the agreement that he give his books to the library. In the following century, further manuscripts were given by Church of Ireland clergymen. Although the twenty-three volumes of medieval manuscripts now at Marsh’s Library form but a tiny part of the overall library, they provide insights into of the roles of intention, opportunity, and personal choice in the formation of this early modern library, which in turn ensured the survival of some medieval manuscripts.

title: Introduction: From Black Famine to the Wildcat Hunger Strike
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Health, care & health workforce; Migration policy, law & governance
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This introduction examines the cultural reception of Gandhian and Irish Republican hunger strikes circa World War 1. In 1922 W. Norman Brown in this journal dichotomized hunger striking into practices diversely legitimated by a precolonial moral economy (Gandhian) and military instrumentalism (Irish Republican). This binary analytically pivots between the processual dimension of striking as expressive ritual versus stressing the political justification of self-harm as a weapon of war. As in all such binary diagrams these dichotomies were descriptively inadequate. Irish Republican public culture rescripted the hunger striker as allegorically incarnating the nineteenth-century famine in colonial Ireland as British genocide. Moving beyond the dichotomies of moral economy versus instrumentalist action, Miguel Abensour proposes that the wildcat labor strike (grève sauvage) exemplifies Claude Lefort's “savage democracy.” The death fast, considered as a wildcat strike, mobilizes tactics and emblems of self-disincorporation to dramatize and accelerate the disincorporation of concentrationist power such as mass incarceration, migrant detention centers, gulags and lagers, militarized borders and apartheid checkpoints. The self-inflicted wildcat strike savages the body of the hunger striker molding it into a conduit for the savaging of programs of disciplinary normation. In the wildcat strike the hunger striker is both above themselves as agent and below themselves as patient at the same time, thereby closing the circle of subjugation and self-determination.

title: Unexpected Origins: Mapping Assisted Female Immigrants to New South Wales
themes: Health, care & health workforce; Education, children & young people; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: During the transition from convict societies to free settler colonies, the Australian colonies encouraged immigration by young, unmarried, working-class women to fill labor shortages and to marry into the community. The tens of thousands of women and girls who arrived under these schemes over the course of the nineteenth century fundamentally changed colonial society. New digital tools for compiling, analyzing, and visualizing data on these women permit closer examination of the characteristics of the group, and of individual outliers. Using historical shipping records, this article delves into the places of origin for 3,768 women and children who arrived on subsidized passages in Sydney between 1848 and 1887. Digital maps confirm the overwhelming predominance of immigrants from the United Kingdom and Ireland. The visualizations also highlight a minority of immigrants from other parts of the world, uncovering new patterns of colonial connections, multi-stage journeys, and return migration which complicate the narrative of female assisted migration.

title: 'Friends of the Country and of the Government': Irish America, the Irish Government, and the Northern Irish Civil Rights Movement
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life
found_in: SemanticScholar:S2_terms_and_Ireland; SemanticScholar:S2_terms_and_Ireland; Crossref:Crossref:q:immigrants Irish; Crossref:Crossref:q:immigrants Irish

abstract: ABSTRACT:From the beginning of 1969, panicked Irish diplomats based across the United States beseeched Iveagh House, the headquarters for the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs, to release an updated policy on raising Northern Ireland as an issue at the United Nations Security Council. These requests resulted from an influx of pressure from Irish Americans who were becoming increasingly concerned about the unfolding situation in Northern Ireland. Following the heavily publicised scenes from Derry on 5 October 1968, which showed police officers beating and dragging civil rights protestors on the city's streets, Irish American interest in the Northern Irish civil rights movement proliferated across the country and across different sections of the diasporic community. While historians have found that the Irish government neglected to effectively monitor the emerging civil rights movement in Northern Ireland, Irish diplomats in the US paid careful attention to how Irish Americans felt about and reacted to the nascent movement in Northern Ireland from early on. Using government documents from the Irish Department of Foreign Affairs, this article examines the reaction from the Irish embassy and consulates to Irish American lobbying, analysing how factors such as class, political ideology and attitudes towards national identity differentiated these responses. This article argues that fissures in the relationship between the state and sections of its diaspora in the US, which stemmed from divisions over the Irish Civil War, contributed to the heightened sensitivity towards Irish American attitudes and actions as tensions began to rise in Northern Ireland.

title: The History of a Forgotten Diaspora: The Polish Minority in Ireland, 1945–1957
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Education, children & young people; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migration policy, law & governance; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This article offers the first systematic historical and sociological examination of the Polish diaspora in post-war Ireland, focusing on the period during which the Irish government continued to recognise the Polish government-in-exile in London (until 1957). It identifies and analyses Polish citizens who consciously chose political exile, most of whom came from intellectual and aristocratic circles. Drawing on quantitative data and biographical evidence, the study reconstructs their social and professional backgrounds and situates them within the broader context of Ireland's post-war migration policy toward refugees from Central and Eastern Europe. The findings suggest that while Ireland demonstrated a limited openness to post-war Polish migration, this tolerance was largely confined to members of the higher social strata. Applicants from working-class backgrounds faced considerable administrative barriers, including frequent refusals of entry visas. The article further reveals that the Polish community in Ireland remained small and socially reserved, displaying minimal political or civic engagement. Exceptions were found among Polish students who contributed to academic and cultural life in Irish institutions. Overall, the diaspora tended to view its presence on the island as temporary, leading most members, after several years, to continue their migration elsewhere

title: Anxieties of Belonging: Ulster Protestant Migrants and the Troubles in Late Imperial England
authors: B. Hazley; Jack Crangle; Graham Dawson; Liam Harte; Fearghus Roulston
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: MANUAL: Ulster Protestant migrants in post-war England
abstract: Abstract Based on the findings of a major oral history study, this article uses the personal narratives of Ulster Protestant migrants to illuminate some of the understudied cultural and human impacts of the Northern Ireland Troubles for postwar British society. Situating these impacts within the history of “internal decolonization” and the postwar implosion of “Greater Britain,” it shows how the Troubles fueled popular perceptions of Northern Ireland as an “imperial liability,” creating distinctive dilemmas of belonging for Ulster Britons settling in England during the period. Drawing on cultural and psychoanalytic approaches to oral history analysis, the article demonstrates how the “composure” of Ulster Protestant subjectivities in Troubles-era England involved attempts to narratively integrate the destabilizing impacts of cultural encounter with memories, emotions, and identifications extending from migrants’ formative experiences of growing up in the polarized sociopolitical world of Northern Ireland. In analyzing the interplay between these contexts and dynamics, the article sheds new light on the cultural legacies of the Troubles for British society, suggesting new ways of situating the conflict within the historiography of postwar Britain and presenting some alternative interpretive possibilities for writing the human history of the Troubles beyond the “flattening rubric of identity.”

title: Late 19th-century connections between Irish psychological medicine and the West Riding Asylum, Wakefield, England.
themes: Asylum, international protection & reception; Health, care & health workforce; Education, children & young people; Migration policy, law & governance
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This paper traces the career trajectories of four Irish doctors - Edward Mazière Courtenay, Oscar Woods, Edward Levinge, and James Wallis - all of whom gained early clinical experience in psychological medicine whilst working at the West Riding Asylum in Wakefield, England, during the 1870s, the era during which this county asylum for paupers aspired to be a "research school" for the study of insanity. An attempt is made to examine whether, as a result of their experiences at Wakefield, these clinicians introduced research practices or any of the innovations of the West Riding Asylum, such as a dedicated pathological laboratory, into the Irish public system of district asylums. The evidence indicates that no such developments occurred in Ireland, despite two of the four clinicians, Courtenay and Woods, achieving positions of considerable authority within the profession on their return to Ireland. Possible reasons for this absence of research in Irish asylums during the latter part of the 19th century are explored.

title: Racialised from the past: Irish genealogies of slavery in the Caribbean
themes: Naturalisation & citizenship; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Migrant communities, identity & family life

abstract: The 2004 Citizenship referendum is a telling index of the nation's sentiment about who is entitled to be Irish. Whether newly arrived or born here Black inhabitants are refused the right to call Ireland home. The exclusion of blackness from constructions of Irishness is strikingly reminiscent of the absence or erasure of black people from Irish diasporic history, particularly in the Americas. This article examines Irish involvement in Caribbean slavery and argues that the slow violence of colonial ideologies of race and race-making contributes to epistemologies of ‘race’ and the exclusion of Blackness from Irish diasporic identity and contemporary national belonging. Irish historiography rarely acknowledges the overlapping processes of Irish migration whitening strategies and African slavery. My inquiry focuses on the connected lives of Irish and African descended women in the Spanish colony of Cuba. Drawing on interdisciplinary scholarship of slavery, race and gender and reading across the myriad relations between people from Europe and Africa in the Caribbean, this article demonstrates the omission of diasporic complicity in slavery from Irish historiography and in doing so challenges the epistemic erasure of Black people in Irish academic knowledge production.

title: Coens, Leavys, and others: anglicisation, assimilation, and “Jewish” surnames in Ireland in the early 20th Century
themes: Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: ABSTRACT Anglicisation in this context is the assimilation of names into the dominant English culture, whether for Jewish immigrants or native Gaels. Biblical names were present in Ireland via both Christianity and English immigration before the period under consideration here, while the process of anglicisation of Gaelic names led to the emergence of surnames in Ireland that are typically regarded as Jewish elsewhere, at a time when there were effectively no Jews in Ireland. The arrival of 5000 Jews in the late nineteenth century, many bearing variants of those names, led to an enrichment of the range of names in the country in a political era when names were regarded as an important signifier of cultural and political identity. The legacy of that enrichment has remained throughout the twentieth century and beyond.

title: The “Irish question” and the National Front: the challenge of British loyalism during the early Troubles, 1969–75
themes: Labour market, work & permits; Health, care & health workforce; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: ABSTRACT The outbreak of the Troubles represented a crisis and opportunity for the fledgling National Front. Unlike other British parties, the “Irish Question” remained an important ideological preoccupation of the National Front. It conspiratorially saw the conflict as a deliberate attempt by international forces to undermine the British nation. This unscored the party’s advocacy of staunch British loyalism, which influenced its propaganda output and saw the party organise pro-loyalist demonstrations in English cities. But these activities failed to capture the same levels of support among the public as its anti-immigration campaigning had. Meanwhile, the National Front’s entanglement with Ulster loyalism in Northern Ireland proved unfruitful. Their respective visions of loyalism proved irreconcilable, illuminating the fundamentally different worldviews of the British far right and Ulster loyalists.

title: Hidden Terrors
themes: Labour market, work & permits; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Between 1832 and 1836, the bacteria Vibrio cholerae caused numerous episodes of mass mortality in cities, small towns, prisons, worksites, and plantations throughout the United States. These outbreaks were part of a larger global pandemic, which occurred before the discovery that sewage-contaminated water spread the disease. Believing their nation to be filled with prosperous, self-disciplined, and independent citizens, Americans of perceived respectability and influence imagined that cholera would find few victims among them, especially when compared to the tyrannical regimes of Asia and Europe, which kept teeming masses in a state of dependence and degradation. They were wrong. Cholera thrived in Jackson’s America. Causing massive diarrhea, painful spasms, blue skin, and death within twenty-four hours of symptoms, Vibrio produced horrifying scenes. The disease not only found victims among the poor and oppressed, of which the US had plenty—recently arrived Irish immigrants, enslaved African Americans, and dispossessed Indigenous peoples—but struck down people of all ranks and inflicted heavy losses in communities thought to be safe. Through the pandemic’s duration, however, powerful people used their public voices to minimize and obscure what was a terrifying reality for diverse Americans. Temperance advocates, medical authorities, newspaper editors, and civic leaders attributed deaths to individual failings, especially drinking alcohol, and disregarded the injustices that enhanced vulnerability. They ignored the numerous deaths among their own ranks, stuck to a delusive narrative that blinded Americans to contradictions to their democracy, and denied a shared humanity that united all people amid the threat of a mysterious killer.

title: Where will this violent force appear next? Military veterans of the Middle East and the racialized policing of migration in the American midwest
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Migration policy, law & governance
screening_note: no sign of empirical data; historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: Against a backdrop of anti-immigration state violence in the American Midwest (e.g., in Chicago and Minneapolis), this article examines the transfer of racialized violence from sites of war to internal policing. The growing recruitment of military veterans into federal law enforcement—particularly The U.S. Department for Homeland Security (DHS) forces: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)—facilitates the spread of practices and ideologies from war zones to the civilian policing of US cities. Drawing on the concept of coloniality, the article explores how racialized cultures of military othering in wars in the Middle East take form in the logics of immigration enforcement ‘at home’, following a boomerang trajectory. Going beyond this and adopting an approach of ‘relational comparison’, the article turns focus on the historical example of British veterans of the First World War in the Royal Irish Constabulary during the Irish War of Independence (1919–1922) who became notorious as the ‘Black-and-Tans’ for their practices of militarized and racialized violence in Ireland. After 1922, this culture and capacity for violence moved on to British Mandate Palestine and beyond (e.g., Kenya, Malaysia, and Hong Kong). The article formulates and responds to the erotema ‘where will this violent force appear next?’ to learn from this precedent and to remain alert to the foreboding inevitability that the carceral and lethal capacities of the DHS are poised for future violent interventions in the US and elsewhere.

title: To this small island: Immigrants and immigration in early medieval Ireland
themes: Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Migration policy, law & governance
venue: Proceedings of the Royal Irish Academy Archaeology Culture History Literature
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract:
To date, relatively little attention has been paid to immigration as a feature
of early medieval Irish society, or to the experience of immigrants in early
medieval Ireland. This is in spite of the fact that immigrants and immigration are both well attested across a variety of extant sources from the period,
including histories and chronicles, legal texts, sagas, hagiography, and the
archaeological record. This article surveys these diverse sources to highlight
the scope and significance of immigration in early Ireland. Within the limits
imposed by the sources, it examines the different kinds of immigrants who
came to Ireland in the early period in terms of their social status (before and
after their migration), gender, and ethnicity, as well as the motives that brought
them to Ireland, their experiences as immigrants, and local attitudes toward
them. It demonstrates the considerable diversity that characterised both the
immigrants themselves and their experiences.

title: Alcoholism, Domestic Violence and Murder: Assessing English Sentiments of Irish Immigrants in the Nineteenth Century
themes: Health, care & health workforce; Migrant communities, identity & family life
venue: Transactions of the Historic Society of Lancashire and Cheshire
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: The migration and settlement account of the McKerney family in Lancashire from 1855 acts as a case study in this article to reflect on English sentiments towards Irish immigrants in the mid-to-late nineteenth century following the economic hardship caused by the Great Famine. After starting a new life in England free of starvation and disease, several members of the McKerney family suffered from alcoholism, domestic violence, mental illness and crime while living in the slums of Preston’s Irish quarter. This article examines two murder cases involving members of the McKerney family in 1876 and 1887 that symbolised several Irish stereotypes widely circulated during the period, revealing underlying negative sentiments towards the Irish in the ways the authorities investigated the murders and the local press portrayed those involved. The dramatic events in the McKerney family history serve as a springboard to explore broader themes in the history of Irish immigration to England, including the illustration of nuanced points of othering experienced by the Irish.

title: Northern France to Ulster: the Lisburn Huguenots revisited
themes: Labour market, work & permits; Attitudes, racism, discrimination & far right; Integration, housing, welfare & inclusion; Emigration, diaspora & return; Migrant communities, identity & family life
screening_note: historical study (subject before 1960) - listed in the historical appendix
abstract: This article reassesses the origins and development of the Huguenot colony established in Lisburn at the turn of the eighteenth century under the leadership of Louis Crommelin. Dispatched to Ireland in 1698 by Henri de Massue de Ruvigny to improve the linen industry, Crommelin settled in Lisburn – with him a group of skilled migrants who formed the core of the colony. Drawing on church records from France, Ireland, the Netherlands and England, this study re-examines the colony’s formation within its broader social, religious and economic contexts. Particular attention is given to the community’s origins in Saint Quentin, northern France, where a shared Protestant identity fostered strong cohesion and shaped patterns of migration. By integrating sources from Saint Quentin, the Netherlands and Lisburn, the study highlights the importance of kinship networks alongside occupational expertise. Migration is shown to have been closely linked to Crommelin’s patronage and extended family connections, which fostered continuity and integration in a new environment. This approach offers a deeper understanding of the community’s origins and reveals previously unexplored relationships, enabling a more precise reconstruction of this distinctive Huguenot micro-diaspora. It further illustrates how migrant communities relied on intertwined kinship and professional networks to facilitate settlement and integration.
